moduleTitle: The oneness of humanity and the equality of all, including the equality of women with men

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.1 Beliefs about the nature of human life: belief in the oneness of humanity and in the equality of all, including complete equality of women with men.
note.summary:
THE ONENESS OF HUMANITY
Sikhs believe that all humans come from the One God (Ik Onkar) and that God's light (jot) shines in every person. Humanity is therefore one family:
• 'The One God is our father; we are the children of the One' (Guru Arjan, Ang 611).
• 'From the One Light, the entire universe welled up; so who is good and who is bad?' (Bhagat Kabir, Ang 1349–50).
• 'No one is my enemy and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone' (Guru Arjan, Ang 1299).
• Guru Gobind Singh wrote 'Recognise the whole human race as one' ('Manas kee jaat sabhai ekai pahchaanbo') – in the Akal Ustat in the Dasam Granth (not the Guru Granth Sahib).

EQUALITY OF ALL
• Caste (jati) is rejected: 'Recognise the Lord's Light within all, and do not ask about caste; there is no caste in the world hereafter' (Ang 349).
• Religion: Guru Nanak's first teaching after the river Bein was 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' – meaning all are equally God's people. The Guru Granth Sahib includes hymns of Hindu and Muslim saints.
• Wealth and status: rich and poor sit together in the sangat and langar.

COMPLETE EQUALITY OF WOMEN WITH MEN
• Spiritual equality – women have the same soul and light and can attain mukti.
• Guru Nanak: 'From woman, man is born… So why call her inferior? From her, kings are born' (Asa di Var, Ang 473).
• Guru Amar Das spoke against sati (widow-burning) and purdah (veiling/seclusion) and appointed women as well as men to teach and lead communities.
• The Sikh Rehat Maryada allows women to take part in every religious function: reading the Guru Granth Sahib, kirtan, Ardas, serving as granthi; women take amrit and are named Kaur.
• Role models: Mata Khivi (langar), Mata Gujri, Mata Sahib Kaur (mother of the Khalsa), Mai Bhago (warrior, 1705).

DIVERSITY / CONTEMPORARY ISSUES
• Practice does not always match teaching: some gurdwaras are associated with particular caste groups (e.g. Ramgarhia gurdwaras in the UK); some families still face cultural pressures such as son-preference or dowry.
• Debate about women serving as Panj Pyare and performing kirtan at the Harimandir Sahib.
• Bibi Jagir Kaur became the first woman president of the SGPC in 1999.
• Many Sikhs campaign against gender discrimination, citing Ang 473.

WHY IT MATTERS
Equality affects worship (everyone covers heads and sits on the floor), langar, sewa, attitudes to other faiths and social justice.

KEY TERMS: Ik Onkar, jot, jati (caste), sangat, langar, Kaur, Sikh Rehat Maryada, sati, purdah.

questions.question:
Which one of the following quotations from the Guru Granth Sahib is used to support the equality of women?
A 'This human body has been given to you'
B 'So why call her inferior? From her, kings are born'
C 'You shall harvest what you plant'
D 'In the realm of truth the Formless Lord abides'
questions.modelAnswer: B – 'So why call her inferior? From her, kings are born' (Guru Nanak, Asa di Var, Ang 473). Guru Nanak argued that women give birth to all people, including kings, so it is wrong to regard them as lesser. The other quotations are about human life, karma and Sach Khand.
evidence: 'So kio manda aakhiai jit jameh rajaan' – Ang 473
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
Which one of the following best expresses the Sikh belief in the oneness of humanity?
A All humans are the same caste
B All humans come from the One God and share the same divine light
C Only Sikhs carry God's light
D People are equal only after initiation
questions.modelAnswer: B – All humans come from the One God and share the same divine light. Bhagat Kabir writes 'From the One Light, the entire universe welled up; so who is good and who is bad?' (Ang 1349–50). The other options either limit God's light or confuse equality with caste or initiation.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one reason why Sikhs believe all people are equal.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: all people were created by the One God (Ik Onkar); God's light (jot) is in every person; God is the father of all ('We are the children of the One' – Ang 611); in God's court there is no caste (Ang 349); the Gurus taught and showed equality.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give one example of how Sikh teaching rejected discrimination against women.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: Guru Amar Das condemned sati (widow-burning); he discouraged purdah/veiling; women may lead worship and read the Guru Granth Sahib; Guru Nanak's teaching 'why call her inferior?' (Ang 473); women can be initiated into the Khalsa and are given the name Kaur; widows may remarry.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the oneness of humanity influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Sikhs welcome everyone into the gurdwara and the langar, whatever their religion, race or social background. Everyone sits on the floor together to eat the same food, which shows that no one is higher or lower than anyone else.

Second way: Sikhs help people in need regardless of who they are. For example, Sikh charities such as Khalsa Aid provide food and shelter to refugees and disaster victims of every faith, because they see God's light in all humans.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two different ways in which Sikhs show the equality of men and women.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: In worship, women and men have the same religious roles. A woman may be a granthi, read from the Guru Granth Sahib, perform kirtan or lead Ardas, because Sikh teaching gives women complete spiritual equality.

Second way: In identity and initiation, women are treated equally. Women can take amrit and wear the five Ks, and are given the name Kaur, which means they do not have to take a husband's or father's family name and have their own dignity as members of the Khalsa.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about the equality of all people.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: All people come from the One God and contain God's light (jot). Since God is the parent of all, everyone is part of one human family and deserves equal respect, whatever their religion, race or nationality.

Second teaching: Caste and social status have no value in God's eyes. Sikhs reject the caste system, since what matters is a person's devotion and actions, not the family they were born into.

Source: Guru Nanak teaches: 'Recognise the Lord's Light within all, and do not ask about caste; there is no caste in the world hereafter' (Ang 349). Guru Arjan also writes 'The One God is our father; we are the children of the One' (Ang 611). These apply directly: if all are children of one father, caste divisions are false.
evidence: 'Ek pita ekas ke ham baarik' – Ang 611
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about the status of women.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Women are completely equal to men spiritually. Women contain the same divine light, can achieve mukti, and can take part fully in worship and leadership. No ritual is closed to women in Sikh teaching.

Second teaching: Women should be respected and not treated as impure or inferior. Guru Nanak rejected ideas that women are polluting (for example during menstruation or after childbirth), and Guru Amar Das opposed practices such as sati and purdah that harmed women.

Source: Guru Nanak writes in Asa di Var: 'From woman, man is born… So why call her inferior? From her, kings are born' (Ang 473). This applies both teachings: since all humans, even rulers, owe their lives to women, it is wrong to treat women as less valuable.
evidence: 'So kio manda aakhiai jit jameh rajaan' – Ang 473
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
“Women and men are completely equal in Sikhism today.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

In Sikh teaching, women and men are spiritually identical: both contain God's light, can achieve mukti and can do every religious role. Guru Nanak asked 'why call her inferior? From her, kings are born' (Ang 473). The Sikh Rehat Maryada allows women to be granthis, to perform kirtan, read the Guru Granth Sahib and lead Ardas.

Women are initiated into the Khalsa in the same way as men and are given the name Kaur, which gives them an independent identity. History provides strong role models: Mata Khivi ran the langar with Guru Angad and is praised in the Guru Granth Sahib (Ang 967); Mai Bhago led soldiers into battle in 1705; Mata Sahib Kaur is seen as the 'mother of the Khalsa'.

In modern times women hold senior positions: Bibi Jagir Kaur became the first woman president of the SGPC (the committee that manages historic gurdwaras in Punjab) in 1999, and many UK gurdwara committees include women.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

In practice, equality is not complete. Women are rarely chosen as Panj Pyare at Amrit ceremonies, and there have been disputes about whether women may perform kirtan inside the Harimandir Sahib, which has traditionally been done by men. Most granthis and gurdwara committee leaders are still men.

Cultural attitudes from Punjabi society, rather than Sikh teaching, still affect some families – such as preference for sons, pressure over dowry, and expectations that women do most of the cooking in langar. Campaigners within the Sikh community have challenged these practices.

Some argue that roles can be equal without being identical, and that women in some families choose different roles freely. Others see this as an excuse for inequality.

CONCLUSION

Sikh teaching clearly supports complete equality of women and men, and that equality is visible in worship, initiation and naming. However, in some areas of practice and culture, especially leadership and Panj Pyare, equality has not been fully achieved. The fairest judgement is that Sikhism teaches complete equality, but Sikhs today are still working to make practice match the Gurus' teaching.
evidence: Debate over women in Panj Pyare and kirtan at Harimandir Sahib
questions.examTip: Use the four bullets: refer to Sikh teaching, argue for the statement, argue for a different view, and reach a justified conclusion. Develop each argument into a chain of reasoning (because... this means... therefore...). Up to 3 extra SPaG marks are available, so use specialist Punjabi terms accurately.

questions.question:
“Belief in the oneness of humanity is the most important teaching in Sikhism.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

The oneness of humanity follows directly from Ik Onkar: if there is one God who created all and whose light is in all, then all people are one family. Kabir's verse 'From the One Light, the entire universe welled up; so who is good and who is bad?' (Ang 1349–50) is central to Sikh identity.

It shapes almost every Sikh practice. Langar, where everyone eats together on the floor; the four doors of the Harimandir Sahib open to all directions; the inclusion of Hindu and Muslim saints in the Guru Granth Sahib; the abolition of caste in the Khalsa – all express this belief. Without it, Sikhism would lose its most distinctive social message.

It is also very relevant today, in a world of racism, religious conflict and inequality. Sikh service to people of all backgrounds, such as Khalsa Aid's work with refugees, puts this belief into practice.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Many Sikhs would say belief in God (Ik Onkar) is more important, because the oneness of humanity is a consequence of it. Without one God there would be no single source of human unity. The Mool Mantra, not a teaching about humanity, opens the Guru Granth Sahib.

Others would argue the aim of life – mukti through overcoming haumai and becoming gurmukh – is the most important teaching, since Sikhs believe human life is an opportunity to unite with God (Ang 12). Belief in equality is a way of living that helps reach that goal.

Some also point out that a belief is only as important as its practice. Caste-based gurdwaras and discrimination still exist in some places, which suggests that in practice other teachings may receive more attention. A humanist might agree that human oneness is the most valuable teaching but say it does not depend on God.

CONCLUSION

The oneness of humanity is clearly one of the most important and distinctive teachings, shaping worship, service and identity. But in Sikh thought it flows from belief in Ik Onkar and serves the aim of union with God. So it is best seen as the most important social teaching of Sikhism, while belief in the One God remains the foundation.
evidence: Langar; four doors of Harimandir Sahib
